title: Compact context prefetch econ sketch
content:
Working sketch: compact context prefetch (CCP) and its impact on latency and per-token economics.

Objective:
- Explore a lightweight prefetch strategy for conversational sessions where the server proactively pulls small context KV pages (compact vectors) for likely next-turn tokens to reduce tail latency without blowing up GPU memory and bandwidth.
- Produce quick comparative numbers (p50/p90/p99, and amortized $/1k tokens) for three strategies: baseline (no prefetch), eager-prefetch (fetch full recent context at session start), and adaptive-compact-prefetch (CCP).

Environment & workload:
- Cluster: r4-gpu-p100x2 (representative midline infra for experiments), batching turned on (dynamic batch window = 10ms), multiplexing disabled for this run.
- Model: open-llama-16k-8bit-quantized (served via runtime v0.9.3-rc).
- Mix: 60% short (user prompt < 64 tokens), 30% medium (64-512), 10% long (>512). 35% of sessions are multi-turn (avg turns/session = 4).
- Traffic pattern: Poisson arrival, occasional 400 qps spikes lasting 20–120s (microburst profile).
- Measurement unit: observed server-side generation latency (ms) from request accepted -> final token scalarization. Cost measured as amortized GPU seconds per 1k tokens then converted to $ using $3.50/GPU-hour baseline.

Prefetch strategies defined:
1) baseline: no proactive work; KV cache populated only when a request triggers a generation.
2) eager-prefetch: at session start (first user message) pull the entire last-N-turn embeddings/KV into GPU memory (N=4, approx 4–12 MB, depending on turn length). Protects p99 but increases memory churn and bandwidth.
3) CCP (adaptive-compact-prefetch): heuristic-driven small-prefetch of compacted KV pages: for each active session we prefetch only the top-k tokens' compressed KV signatures (k=128 tokens worth of compacted data, typically 0.6–1.2 MB) when the session is idle for >200ms or when request rate spikes. If request begins, runtime expands prefetched compact to full KV on demand (incremental).

Sampling methodology:
- 30-minute runs per strategy, repeated 5 times; warmup 5 minutes dropped. Reported metrics are medians of the runs.
- Synthetic but replay-like traffic seeded from production sampling (anonymized).
- P99s estimated with bootstrapped confidence intervals (approx ±8% given run length).

Quick numeric summary (median of medians):

Strategy            | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | GPU-s/1k tokens | $/1k tokens
--------------------|---------|---------|---------|-----------------|-----------
baseline             | 78      | 230     | 820     | 0.92            | $0.05
 eage-prefetch       | 82      | 160     | 320     | 1.15            | $0.07
 CCP (adaptive)      | 80      | 175     | 380     | 1.02            | $0.055

Interpretation notes:
- Baseline has lowest steady-state GPU consumption (fewer background transfers) but suffers large p99 tail from on-demand KV loads during microbursts and long-context requests.
- Eager-prefetch reduces tail substantially at the cost of more GPU-seconds because it moves bandwidth earlier and keeps heavier residency in memory. For workloads with long sessions and high locality, eager is attractive; for bursty multi-tenant clusters it inflates steady costs.
- CCP hits much of the tail mitigation of eager-prefetch (p99 reduced ~54% vs baseline) while adding only small GPU overhead (~10% above baseline). CCP appears to be a sweet spot for mixed session workloads.

Ascii chart: relative p99 vs cost (normalized to baseline=1.0)

Strategy      | p99_norm | cost_norm
--------------|----------|----------
baseline       | 1.00     | 1.00
 eager-prefetch| 0.39     | 1.25
 CCP           | 0.46     | 1.10

Microburst behavior (annotated observations):
- Baseline: during 400 qps spike we saw p99 jump to >1s for ~18% of requests; many of those were cold-KV expansions for long sessions.
- Eager: p99 contained to <350ms during spikes but observed resource contention causing small queuing p90 increase (10–12%).
- CCP: during spikes, prefetched compact pages served ~65% of microburst requests without fallback; remaining ~35% triggered incremental expansion which caused p99 jitter but still stayed below baseline heavy tail.

Cost model sensitivity (quick):
- If GPU-hour price doubles, eager-prefetch penalty becomes more visible (cost_norm from 1.25 -> 1.40 in this workload) while CCP scales linearly and remains closer to baseline.
- For a workload where 70% sessions are long (>512 tokens), eager-prefetch wins economically because the extra work amortizes well. (We didn't run that variant here; follow-up test recommended.)

Operational considerations / caveats:
- CCP requires fast compaction/decompaction paths in the runtime; if these are implemented in Python or cross-host RPCs, the latency wins evaporate. Ensure compaction is GPU-local or very high-throughput host-side.
- Memory pressure: CCP reduces peak memory compared to eager-prefetch but increases transient bandwidth; network-attached NVMe prefetchers may be impacted.
- Failure modes: CCP increases complexity for cache invalidation and staleness when rollouts change model KV formats. Add feature-gate + rollout plan.

Recommendations (next steps):
- Run a targeted test with 70% long-session mix to validate the amortization crossover point. (Jira: SRT-889)
- Prototype CCP in C++ runtime with compaction accelerated kernels; validate end-to-end latency with multiplexing on.
- Add a metric to Console: "compact-prefetch hit rate" and a dashboard for incremental expansion latencies.
- Consider a TTL heuristic (short-lived compacts for low-activity sessions) to bound memory.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is the marginal cost of decompaction on GPU in terms of token throughput? We need microbench per-GPU.
- Interaction with quantization profiles: does compacted KV survive across quantization boundaries? Risky for mixing model variants.
- Security/telemetry: ensure compacted pages do not leak PII; add mask in prefetcher for sensitive tokens.

Appendix: raw per-run numbers (one run example)
- baseline run A: p50=75, p90=218, p99=812, GPU-s/1k=0.89
- eager run A: p50=83, p90=158, p99=308, GPU-s/1k=1.12
- ccp run A: p50=79, p90=171, p99=374, GPU-s/1k=1.01

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally rough — want feedback on the heuristics and whether we should prioritize CCP implementation vs more aggressive eager-prefetch for enterprise Dedicated customers (who value predictable tail).
- If you want plots, I can export the CSVs and produce quick matplotlib charts.

Tagged issues for follow up: SRT-889, PERF-712, CON-PRF-21.

-- Avery
